## Status

Discussion document, 2026-09-22. Nothing here is fitted or authorised for a
refit. It answers one question raised in the model review — *can the Whittle
likelihood tell us about slowly wandering amplitudes?* — and then writes down
the model that collects every change agreed in that review, with its fitting
procedure. Every statement about the current model points at the code:
`src/experiments/noise_model/model.py` (parameters and priors,
`class Priors` and `sample_params`), `src/experiments/noise_model/fit.py`
(objective and optimiser), `src/data_processing/noise_model/render.py`
(the renderer). Numbers quoted from fits name their file under
`results/noise_v2/`.
:::

# The short answer

The current model (v2) has **no amplitude wander**: a rendered clip's line
powers and floor shape are fixed by the rig parameters and the rotor-speed
trajectory; only the phases are random
(`render.py`, module docstring). The claim "the Whittle likelihood cannot see
slow wander" is true **of that model** — a constant parameter cannot absorb a
zero-mean fluctuation, so the fluctuation leaves no trace in the fit — and
**false of the model proposed here**, where every block of a few hundred
milliseconds gets its own amplitude latent with a prior centred on the clip's
mean. Each block's periodogram is then fully informative about that block's
amplitude, and the wander's size and memory are the spread and the
autocorrelation of the block latents. It is the floor-spline construction —
a smooth curve with a Gaussian prior — applied along time instead of along
frequency.

The rest of the page is the reasoning at the level of someone who has not met
a periodogram before, then the modified model, then its fit.

# Part 1 — what the likelihood sees

## 1.1 A periodogram cell

Take one microphone, cut the audio into frames of $N = 2048$ samples
(128 ms at 16 kHz), hop 512, window each frame with a Hann taper and take
the Fourier transform. The squared magnitude at frequency bin $f$ of frame
$n$ is one **periodogram cell** $I_m(n, f)$: "how much power was there at
frequency $f$ during frame $n$".

For a Gaussian signal, each cell is a random number whose **mean** is the
signal's power spectral density at that frequency, $S_m(n, f)$, and whose
distribution is exponential:

$$
I_m(n,f) \;\sim\; S_m(n,f)\cdot \mathrm{Exp}(1), \qquad
\mathbb E[I] = S,\quad \operatorname{sd}[I] = S .
$$

So a single cell tells you the local power to within a factor of $e^{\pm 1}$ —
very noisy — and cells at different frequencies (and, for a taper with hop
$\ge N/4$, different frames) are approximately independent.

## 1.2 The Whittle likelihood

Given a model that predicts the density $S_\theta(n, f)$ from parameters
$\theta$, the log-likelihood of all the cells under the exponential law is

$$
\ell(\theta) \;=\; -\sum_{m,n,f}\Big[\log S_\theta(m,n,f) + \frac{I_m(n,f)}{S_\theta(m,n,f)}\Big] .
$$

That is the Whittle likelihood. It is an approximation (it ignores the
correlation between neighbouring cells that the taper introduces) but it is
the standard one for spectral fitting and it is what every v2 fit maximises
(`fit.py`, the objective; the composite variant pools frames of a window that
share a carrier, but the form is the same).

Two properties matter below.

::: {.def}
**(W1) A scale is easy to estimate from many cells.** If $n$ independent
cells share one unknown scale $\theta$ (their model is $S = \theta \cdot
\text{shape}$ with the shape known), the maximum-likelihood estimate is the
mean of the ratios $I/\text{shape}$ and its relative standard deviation is
$1/\sqrt n$. In decibels: $\operatorname{sd} \approx 4.34/\sqrt n$ dB. Ten
cells give $\pm 1.4$ dB, a hundred give $\pm 0.4$ dB.
:::

::: {.def}
**(W2) The likelihood only sees the mean of each cell.** Everything the fit
learns about $\theta$ comes through $S_\theta$. A random effect that changes
the true density from frame to frame but leaves a constant model in place
can only show up as a bias of the constant — not as a separate parameter.
:::

## 1.3 Why the constant-amplitude model is blind

Suppose the true line power at order $k$ of rotor $i$ is not constant but
wanders slowly:

$$
P_{ik}(t) \;=\; \bar P_{ik}\, e^{w_{ik}(t)}, \qquad
w_{ik} \text{ slow, zero-mean, sd } \sigma_w .
$$

The v2 model has one number $\bar P_{ik}$ (well, $p_{ik} = 10\log_{10}\bar P_{ik}$,
site `profile_db`) for the whole pool. Under (W2), the fit's best constant is
the one whose density matches the cells on average, i.e. roughly the
time-mean of $P_{ik}(t)$, which is $\bar P_{ik}\, e^{\sigma_w^2/2}$ — a
slight upward bias. That is all. The **variance** of the wander is invisible:
the cells' spread around their mean is already the exponential law's own
spread, and a model with one constant has nowhere to put an extra spread.
Nothing in `Priors` or `sample_params` corresponds to $\sigma_w$.

Whatever the real amplitude variation is, the current fit therefore either
ignores it or pushes it into a parameter that *can* change the per-frame
density: the line width $\gamma_{ik}$ (a line that fades in and out over
frames looks, in a pooled periodogram, like a broader hump than a steady
line) or the per-mic gains. The degenerate widths found in every fit
(`round5/fits/dregon_room2_floor__flight_profile.json`: 7223 Hz at $k=65$;
`round3/fits/michaels_fly125_cruise__flight.json`: 125 578 Hz at $k=18$ on
rotor 3) are consistent with that escape route, though they also have the
prior explanation given in the model review (a log-normal prior is quadratic
in $\log\gamma$ and charges only ~40 nats for a 7 kHz line).

## 1.4 Why per-block latents make it visible

Now give every **block** $b$ — a group of consecutive frames, say
$T_b = 0.5$ s $\approx 15$ frames — its own amplitude:

$$
P_{ik}(b) \;=\; \bar P_{ik}\, e^{w_{ik}(b)} .
$$

Within the block the model is constant, so the block's cells around line
$(i,k)$ have density $S \propto P_{ik}(b)$ and, by (W1), the Whittle
likelihood of *those cells alone* pins $w_{ik}(b)$ to within
$4.34/\sqrt{n_{ik}(b)}$ dB, where $n_{ik}(b)$ is the number of cells the line
occupies in the block (its frames times the bins it spans). The likelihood
is not "blind" to the block amplitude; it is exactly as informative as the
count of cells allows.

What ties the blocks together is a **prior on the latents**, and that is
where $\sigma_w$ and the wander's memory $\tau_w$ live:

$$
w_{ik}(b+1) \;=\; \rho\, w_{ik}(b) + \sqrt{1-\rho^2}\,\sigma_w\,\varepsilon_b,
\qquad \rho = e^{-T_b/\tau_w},\quad \varepsilon_b \sim \mathcal N(0,1),
$$

an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process sampled at the block rate: stationary sd
$\sigma_w$, correlation time $\tau_w$. This is the same object as the shaft
OU of the phase model and the same object as the floor spline's Gaussian
prior — a smooth random curve with a known covariance — only now the
curve runs over blocks instead of over frequency control points.

**The information flow, in words.** Each block's cells say "my amplitude is
about this, $\pm$ a few dB". The prior says "consecutive blocks differ by
about $\sigma_w\sqrt{2(1-\rho)}$, and all of them hover around the clip's
$\bar P_{ik}$". Combining the two gives (a) a smoothed amplitude track per
line, (b) an estimate of $\bar P_{ik}$ that is *less* biased than the
constant model's, and (c), from the spread and the lag-1 correlation of the
smoothed tracks, the wander parameters $\sigma_w, \tau_w$. Point (c) is what
the legacy model's `harm_gp_std_db` / `harm_gp_tau_s` sliders set by hand
and what v2 lost.

Nothing in this argument is specific to the comb: the floor's 14 spline
control values $c_j$ can carry a block latent $u_j(b)$ in exactly the same
way, which gives the floor level and colour their slow drift back
(the legacy `floor_gp_std_db`, `floor_color_*`).

## 1.5 Where the Whittle likelihood genuinely stops

The block construction removes the blindness, not every limitation. Four
remain and each is a design constraint on the block length and on what is
asked of the fit.

1. **Wander faster than a block is width.** A line whose power changes
   *within* a block is, to that block's periodogram, a broadened line. The
   block must be short against $\tau_w$; the measured order-tracked
   line-power autocorrelation (R4's estimator on real windows) decides
   $T_b$. If the real wander has a fast component, it stays in $\gamma$ —
   and then $\gamma$ is a physical width plus a modulation width, which the
   paper must say.
2. **Few cells, weak line: the latent is prior-dominated.** A line 3 dB over
   the floor spanning 3 bins in a 15-frame block has $n \approx 45$ cells
   but most of their power is floor; the effective count is far smaller.
   The posterior of $w_{ik}(b)$ then follows the prior — the fit will
   report "no evidence of wander" for such lines, not "no wander". Report
   $\sigma_w$ only from orders whose block-level sd is under, say, 2 dB
   (the slider in §1.6 shows the trade).
3. **A moving carrier inside the block smears the line.** The block
   periodogram is computed at fixed frequencies; if the rotor speed moves
   by $\delta$ rev/s across the block, order $k$ moves $k\delta$ Hz and the
   line's power spreads over bins. At 7.8 Hz per bin and a DREGON ramp of
   10 rev/s per second, a 0.5 s block moves order 10 by 50 Hz — six bins.
   Either the block periodogram is **carrier-aligned** (demodulate each
   frame at its own carrier before averaging, the order-domain instrument
   already in `tracking.order_domain`) or blocks are restricted to
   near-constant-speed spans. This is the same label-precision limit that
   set `k_max(T)` in the v2 plan.
4. **Rotors unresolved at low orders are one amplitude, not four.** At
   2048-point frames the four DREGON rotors' $k \le 8$ lines fall in the
   same bins. A per-rotor $w_{ik}(b)$ at those orders is not identifiable;
   only the rotor-sum's block amplitude is. Either share the low-order
   latent across rotors (as `flight_floor_lowk` shared the gain) or fit
   those orders on longer frames.

Beyond these, Whittle keeps its known structural blind spot: it uses the
**magnitude** of each cell and discards the cross-spectrum between
microphones and the phase relation between orders. Amplitude wander is a
magnitude effect, so this does not affect it; it affects the coherence
questions the R3 hump study raised and needs the cross-spectral Whittle
extension if they are ever pursued.

## 1.6 How much wander can a block resolve?

```{ojs}
viewof Tb = Inputs.range([0.1, 4], {value: 0.5, step: 0.1, label: "block length T_b (s)"})
viewof bins = Inputs.range([1, 9], {value: 3, step: 1, label: "bins a line occupies"})
viewof snr = Inputs.range([0, 30], {value: 6, step: 1, label: "line-to-floor ratio at the peak (dB)"})
viewof tauw = Inputs.range([0.5, 20], {value: 3, step: 0.5, label: "wander correlation time tau_w (s)"})
```

```{ojs}
frames = Math.max(1, Math.round(Tb * 16000 / 512))
cells = frames * bins
snrLin = Math.pow(10, snr / 10)
// fraction of a cell's power that belongs to the line, at the peak bin
lineFrac = snrLin / (1 + snrLin)
// effective cells: each cell informs the line scale with weight lineFrac^2 (delta-method)
nEff = cells * lineFrac * lineFrac
sdDb = 4.34 / Math.sqrt(nEff)
rho = Math.exp(-Tb / tauw)
html`<table>
<tr><td>frames per block</td><td>${frames}</td></tr>
<tr><td>cells per line per block</td><td>${cells}</td></tr>
<tr><td>effective cells (floor-diluted)</td><td>${nEff.toFixed(1)}</td></tr>
<tr><td><b>sd of one block's amplitude estimate</b></td><td><b>${sdDb.toFixed(2)} dB</b></td></tr>
<tr><td>block-to-block prior correlation ρ = e^(−T_b/τ_w)</td><td>${rho.toFixed(3)}</td></tr>
<tr><td>smallest wander sd the block can distinguish from noise (≈ sd/√2)</td><td>${(sdDb / Math.SQRT2).toFixed(2)} dB</td></tr>
</table>`
```

Reading: a 6 dB line over three bins in half-second blocks is measured to
about $\pm 1.1$ dB per block, so a wander of $\sigma_w \ge 1$ dB is
resolvable on it; a 0 dB line is not (sd $\pm 3$ dB). Longer blocks buy
precision at the cost of smearing (constraint 1 and 3). The legacy model
drew `harm_gp_std_db` in the 2–6 dB range, which is comfortably above the
threshold on any visible order.

# Part 2 — the modified model

Everything the review agreed, collected. Notation as on the supervisor deck:
mic $m$, rotor $i$ (or $r$), order $k$, block $b$, time $t$. Changes to v2
are marked **[new]**; the rest is v2 unchanged.

## 2.1 The signal

$$
x_m(t) \;=\; \sum_i\sum_k A_{mik}(t)\cos\phi_{ik}(t) \;+\; n_m(t) .
$$

One cosine per (rotor, order), plus broadband noise.

## 2.2 Phase

$$
\phi_{ik}(t) = 2\pi k\!\int_0^t f_i(s)\,ds \;+\; k\,\theta_i(t) \;+\; \psi_{ik}(t) \;+\; \alpha_{ik}
$$

- $f_i(t)$: the rotor's labelled speed (rev/s); given, from telemetry or the
  refined track.
- $\theta_i(t)$: the shaft's integrated speed error, one per rotor, shared by
  all its orders (multiplied by $k$):
  $d\nu_i = -\lambda\nu_i\,dt + \sqrt{2\lambda}\,\sigma_\nu\,dW_i,\;
  d\theta_i = \nu_i\,dt$. The $\sqrt{2\lambda}$ makes $\sigma_\nu$ the
  stationary sd of the speed error in rad/s, independent of $\lambda$ — the
  size and the memory are separate knobs.
- $\psi_{ik}(t)$: a per-line Wiener phase, increments $\mathcal N(0,
  4\pi\gamma_{ik}|\tau|)$, which makes the line a Lorentzian of half-width
  $\gamma_{ik}$ Hz (derivation: $\mathbb E[e^{i\Delta\psi}] = e^{-2\pi\gamma|\tau|}$,
  an exponential autocorrelation, whose transform is a Lorentzian of HWHM
  $\gamma$).
- $\alpha_{ik}$: a fixed random start phase.

**[new] priors.** $\sigma_\nu \sim$ HalfNormal$(s_\nu)$ in rad/s and
$\gamma_{ik}/(\gamma_0 k) \sim$ HalfNormal$(c_\gamma)$, with $\gamma_0 =
0.01$ Hz (the bench decoherence law) and $c_\gamma$ of order 3. Both are
light-tailed in **linear** units: a width of $5\gamma_0 k$ costs 1.4 nats,
$13$ Hz at $k=1$ costs $\sim 10^5$ nats. No truncation — the penalty is
smooth everywhere, so L-BFGS in the unconstrained space never stalls at a
wall — but nothing the data does not demand can be wide. The current
LogNormal$(\log 0.01k,\;1.0)$ is removed.

## 2.3 Line amplitude

$$
A_{mik}(t) \;=\; \sqrt{2\,\bar P_{ik}}\;
\Big(\tfrac{f_i(t)}{f_{\mathrm{ref}}}\Big)^{a/2}\;
e^{w_{ik}(b(t))/2}\;
10^{g_{mi}/20}
$$

- $\bar P_{ik} = 10^{p_{ik}/10}$: the line's mean power at the reference
  speed $f_{\mathrm{ref}} = 80$ rev/s (`profile_db`). The square root
  converts power to amplitude; the $/2$ in the exponents are the same
  conversion.
- $(f_i/f_{\mathrm{ref}})^{a}$: the speed law on power, $a$ = `amp_exp`,
  prior $\mathcal N(2, 1)$, pinned at 2 when the pool's speed span is under
  1.5× (unchanged).
- **[new]** $e^{w_{ik}(b)}$: the block wander of §1.4. Hierarchical:
  $w_{ik}(b) = w_i(b) + v_{ik}(b)$, a per-rotor common part (all orders of a
  rotor breathe together — the legacy `harm_coherence` at 1) and a per-line
  residual; each an OU across blocks with its own $(\sigma, \tau)$:
  $(\sigma_{w}, \tau_{w})$ for $w_i$, $(\sigma_v, \tau_v)$ for $v_{ik}$.
  Priors on the four hyperparameters: HalfNormal on the sds (scale from the
  R4 order-tracked line-power spread on real windows), LogNormal on the
  times centred on the measured autocorrelation time.
- **[new]** $10^{g_{mi}/20}$: the microphone gain of rotor $i$ at mic $m$
  is **not free**. With channel sensitivities normalised in the data
  (pending the rank test of `results/noise_v2/mic_gains/`), it is the
  geometric spreading from the known rotor–mic distances,
  $g_{mi} = -20\log_{10}(d_{mi}/d_{\mathrm{ref}}) + \delta_i$, with at most
  one free directivity offset $\delta_i$ per rotor (prior
  $\mathcal N(0, 3)$ dB). The three v2 blocks `mic_gains_db`,
  `mic_line_gain_db`, `mic_floor_db` (48 numbers, 16 identifiable) are
  removed.

**[new] prior on $p_{ik}$: resolved or below the floor.** Whether order
$(i,k)$ is a *resolved line* is decided on a measurement that can resolve
it — the bench periodogram of the same rotor at its cruise speed, or a
carrier-aligned order-domain estimate on the flight windows — **not** on the
pooled 7.8 Hz/bin flight periodogram (whose "$\ge 2$ dB excess" is met by a
neighbour rotor's line or a floor bump). A resolved order gets
$p_{ik} \sim \mathcal N(\text{measured}, 10)$ as now. An unresolved order
gets a **one-sided** penalty: zero cost anywhere at or below the local floor
level, HalfNormal$(8\ \mathrm{dB})$ on the excess above it. It may sink as
far as it likes; it may not stand up unless the data lifts it. This replaces
the current $\mathcal N(\text{floor}-15, 8)$ parking, which pays to sink
*and* pays to rise.

## 2.4 The floor

$$
S_m(f, t) \;=\;
\Big[\tfrac1R\textstyle\sum_i \big(\tfrac{f_i(t)}{f_{\mathrm{ref}}}\big)^{b} + s\Big]\;
10^{\,C(f,\,b(t))/10}
\;+\; W_m(f)
$$

- The bracket is unchanged: the rotor-mean speed law with exponent $b$
  (`floor_exp`, LN$(\log 2, 0.5)$, pinned on short spans) plus the static
  fraction $s$ (`floor_static_rel`).
- **[new]** $C(f, b)$: the floor shape in dB is **the spline alone**,
  $C(f,b) = \sum_{j=1}^{14} B_j(f)\,c_j(b)$, with $B_j$ the linear
  interpolation weights on the geometric control grid 30 … 8000 Hz. The
  separate mean $\mu_F$ and tilt $t_F$ are dropped: on this grid the spline
  already spans a constant and a straight line in $\log f$, so the three
  were collinear and the fits split them arbitrarily
  (`michaels_fly125_cruise__flight.json`: tilt $-0.04$ dB/oct, spline
  swing $+19 \to -58$ dB, $\|z\| = 13.9$ against a prior expectation of
  3.7). The control values are $c_j(b) = \bar c_j + u_j(b)$:
  - $\bar c_j = \mu + \sigma_B (L z)_j$, $z \sim \mathcal N(0, I)$, $L$ the
    Cholesky factor of the squared-exponential kernel across control points
    (as now), $\mu$ the measured band median, and $\sigma_B$ **measured**
    from the real windows' floor-shape spread rather than a constant — so
    the $z$ prior binds.
  - **[new]** $u_j(b)$: the floor's slow drift, an OU across blocks shared
    by all control points for the level (one latent $u(b)$) plus a
    per-control-point residual for the colour — the same two-level
    structure as the comb wander, with its own $(\sigma_u, \tau_u)$.
- **[new]** $W_m(f)$: a per-microphone **static** term for wind /
  self-noise, with a fixed low-frequency shape (below ~500 Hz) and one free
  level per mic, not scaled by speed, not scaled by a channel gain. Present
  only where the rank test shows the per-mic floor excess is not a channel
  sensitivity (DREGON's floor–comb mic-gain correlation is $-0.39$ with an
  18 dB spread; Michael's is $+0.82$). If the test says the excess is a
  sensitivity, $W_m$ is dropped and the channels are normalised in the data.

## 2.5 What is fitted where

| quantity | per | prior / status |
|---|---|---|
| $p_{ik}$ | rig | resolved: $\mathcal N$(measured, 10 dB); unresolved: one-sided HalfNormal above the floor **[new]** |
| $\gamma_{ik}$ | rig | HalfNormal in linear units, scale $c_\gamma \gamma_0 k$ **[new]** |
| $\sigma_\nu$ | rig | HalfNormal **[new]**; $\lambda$ pinned in flight (unchanged) |
| $a$, $b$, $s$ | rig | unchanged; pinned on short-span pools |
| $\bar c_j$ via $z$, $\mu$ | rig | $\mathcal N(0, I)$ with measured $\sigma_B$; $\mu_F$, $t_F$ removed **[new]** |
| $\delta_i$ | rig | $\mathcal N(0, 3)$ dB; geometry gives the rest **[new]** |
| $W_m$ level | rig (per mic) | only if the rank test demands it **[new]** |
| $w_i(b)$, $v_{ik}(b)$, $u(b)$, $u_j(b)$ | clip × block | OU latents **[new]** |
| $\sigma_w, \tau_w, \sigma_v, \tau_v, \sigma_u, \tau_u$ | rig | HalfNormal / LogNormal, centred on measured statistics **[new]** |

# Part 3 — fitting, line by line

## 3.1 Data

1. Windows of real audio with a rotor-speed label: the same supports as v2
   (`experiments.noise_model.supports`), 8 microphones, 16 kHz.
2. Each window → frames ($N = 2048$, hop 512, periodic Hann) → periodogram
   cells $I_m(n, f)$, one per (mic, frame, bin), in the units the forward
   model uses (`spectrum.py`'s work-grid convention). Bins in the fit band
   30 – 7900 Hz.
3. **[new]** Frames are grouped into blocks of $T_b$ seconds. $T_b$ is not a
   free parameter: it is set from the measured autocorrelation time of
   order-tracked line power on real windows (R4's estimator) at roughly
   $\tau_w/4$, and checked against constraint 3 of §1.5 (carrier motion
   inside a block under one bin at the highest fitted order; blocks that
   violate it are dropped or carrier-aligned).
4. Per frame, the carriers $f_i(n)$ from the label; per block, the
   block-mean carriers and the speed factors.

## 3.2 The forward model of a block

For block $b$ of a window, the model predicts the density at every (mic,
bin):

$$
S_m(b, f) \;=\; \sum_i \sum_k P_{ik}(b)\,10^{g_{mi}/10}\;\mathcal L_{ik}\big(f - k\bar f_i(b)\big)
\;+\; S^{\text{floor}}_m(b, f)
$$

- $P_{ik}(b) = \bar P_{ik}\,(\bar f_i(b)/f_{\mathrm{ref}})^{a}\,e^{w_{ik}(b)}$.
- $\mathcal L_{ik}$ is the line shape: the Lorentzian of half-width
  $\gamma_{ik}$ convolved with the shaft's Gaussian core of sd
  $k\sigma_\nu/2\pi$ Hz and with the frame window's transform — exactly the
  R3 line-shape kernel `spectrum.py` evaluates now, unchanged.
- $S^{\text{floor}}_m(b, f)$ is §2.4 with $C(f, b)$ at the block's control
  values and the block-mean speed factor.

This is the current `flight_model` with two extra inputs per block, the
latent vectors $w(b)$ and $u(b)$. Nothing else in the forward model changes.

## 3.3 The objective

$$
\mathcal J \;=\; \underbrace{\sum_{\text{windows}}\sum_{m,b,n\in b,f}\Big[\log S_m(b,f) + \tfrac{I_m(n,f)}{S_m(b,f)}\Big]}_{\text{Whittle, per block}}
\;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{\text{latents}} \tfrac12\, \mathbf w^\top \Sigma_{\text{OU}}^{-1}\mathbf w}_{\text{block priors}}
\;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{\text{rig params}} -\log \pi(\theta)}_{\text{rig priors}}
$$

Line by line:

1. **Whittle per block.** Every frame $n$ inside block $b$ is compared to
   the block's density $S_m(b, f)$. The frames of a block share the latent,
   the blocks of a window share the rig parameters, the windows of a rig
   share everything but the latents.
2. **Block priors.** For each latent track (one per rotor for $w_i$, one per
   line for $v_{ik}$, one for $u$, one per control point for $u_j$), the OU
   quadratic form: with $\rho = e^{-T_b/\tau}$ and $B$ blocks,
   $\tfrac12\big[w_1^2/\sigma^2 + \sum_{b\ge 2}(w_b - \rho w_{b-1})^2/(\sigma^2(1-\rho^2))\big]
   + \tfrac{B}{2}\log\sigma^2 + \tfrac{B-1}{2}\log(1-\rho^2)$.
   The two log terms are what let $\sigma$ and $\tau$ be fitted at all: a
   small $\sigma$ makes the quadratic cheap but the $\log\sigma^2$ term
   expensive, and the optimum sits where the latents' actual spread equals
   $\sigma$.
3. **Rig priors.** The list of §2.5, each as $-\log$ density in the
   unconstrained parametrisation Pyro uses (HalfNormal via a softplus /
   absolute-value bijector, LogNormal via $\log$).

::: {.callout-warning}
## The one place joint MAP is known to cheat

Maximising $\mathcal J$ jointly over the latents **and** their variance
hyperparameters $\sigma_w, \sigma_v, \sigma_u$ underestimates the variances:
the latents shrink toward zero and the hyperparameter follows them (the
classic random-effects MAP bias — the same reason a sample variance divides
by $n-1$). Two remedies, either acceptable:

- **Fix the correlation times** $\tau$ from the R4 autocorrelation
  measurement and estimate the sds by **moment matching** after the fit:
  $\hat\sigma^2 = $ the sample variance of the MAP latents *plus* the mean
  posterior variance of a latent (from the block-level Fisher information
  of §1.6, $\approx (4.34/\sqrt{n_{\text{eff}}})^2$ in dB²). Simple,
  transparent, and the correction is exactly the quantity the slider shows.
- **Marginalise** the latents with a Laplace approximation (integrate the
  Gaussian prior against a quadratic expansion of the block Whittle term
  around its optimum) and maximise the marginal in the hyperparameters.
  Standard (it is what `lme4`-style software does), one extra Hessian per
  block, no bias.

The first is the recommended starting point; the second is the check.
:::

## 3.4 The optimisation

1. **Parametrisation.** All rig parameters and all latents live in one
   unconstrained vector: Pyro sites as now (`sample_params`), with the
   latents as additional `to_event` sites inside a per-window plate. An
   8 s window at $T_b = 0.5$ s has 16 blocks; with $R = 4$, $K = 88$ that
   is $16\,(4 + 4\cdot 88 + 1 + 14) \approx 5\,900$ latents per window.
   L-BFGS handles that; what it cannot handle is a pool of 250 windows
   with all latents free at once, so:
2. **Alternation.** (i) With latents at zero, fit the rig parameters on the
   pool exactly as v2 does (warm start from the current fits — their
   profile, floor and mic values are usable once re-expressed in the new
   parametrisation). (ii) With rig parameters fixed, fit each window's
   latents independently — the windows decouple, so this is 250 small
   L-BFGS problems, embarrassingly parallel on `uni-cpu`. (iii) Re-fit the
   rig parameters with the latents fixed. (iv) Update $\sigma$'s by moment
   matching (§3.3 box). Repeat (ii)–(iv) until the Whittle term moves by
   less than the v2 tolerance ($10^{-4}$ nats/cell). Three to five rounds
   in practice for this kind of model; each round is one `uni-cpu` job.
3. **Restarts and pins** as v2: four seeds, the speed-law span pin, $\lambda$
   pinned in flight. The half-normal priors make the restarts far less
   necessary — the width degeneracy that produced the restart spread is
   gone — but they stay as the convergence check.
4. **Convergence label** on every fit as now (`which_converged`).

## 3.5 What to check before believing it

1. **Prior predictive.** Render the prior alone (no data) and confirm no
   line wider than a few $\gamma_0 k$ and no floor swing beyond the measured
   $\sigma_B$ appears — the priors now forbid the v2 pathologies by
   construction, and this is the test that they do.
2. **Held-out statistic.** The R4 order-tracked line-power spread across
   frames within a window, on real windows **not** in the pool, against the
   same statistic on renders from the fit. v2 cannot match it (it renders
   zero spread); the new fit's $\sigma_w, \sigma_v$ should.
3. **The tonality audit** (`results/noise_v2/rig_sampler/tonality/`) on the
   refitted rigs, now on rendered audio as well as on the expectation.
4. **The parity gate** unchanged (HPPNet on renders vs real), with the
   caveat already recorded that it measures familiarity, not transfer; the
   transfer test is a retrained arm.

# Part 4 — what this does not decide

- Whether the rotor-speed label needs its own per-rotor deviation track in
  DREGON free flight (the R5 follow-up). The block construction reduces the
  damage of label error (a block whose carrier is off just gets a wrong
  alignment for that block) but does not remove it; the carrier-aligned
  block periodogram of §1.5 (3) is the cheap mitigation.
- Cross-microphone coherence and inter-order phase relations: outside the
  Whittle magnitude likelihood, unchanged from v2.
- The trajectory model, the regime composition, the speed-law pins: all
  unchanged.

::: {.callout-note}
## Decisions taken in the review (2026-09-22), for the record

1. Half-normal, linear-space priors on $\gamma_{ik}$ and $\sigma_\nu$; no
   truncation.
2. Orders not resolved on a resolving measurement may sink below the floor
   at no cost.
3. Slow amplitude wander restored: per-block OU latents for line power
   (rotor-common + per-line) and for the floor spline (level + colour), with
   fitted or moment-matched hyperparameters.
4. Floor shape = spline only; $\mu_F$ and $t_F$ removed; $\sigma_B$ measured.
5. Channel gains: normalise in the data if the rank test holds; comb mic
   gains from geometry; a per-mic static wind term only where the floor
   excess is not a channel sensitivity.
6. No refit is started until authorised.
:::
